data.statement: Hebrews identifies Jesus as High Priest according to the order of Melchizedek.
data.disputed: No — regarding what Hebrews explicitly states
data.interpretive_divergence: Begins when determining the ecclesiological implications of the claim.

data.statement: Jeremiah announces a new covenant that is not like the covenant made at Sinai.
data.disputed: No — regarding what Jeremiah explicitly states
data.interpretive_divergence: Divergence concerns whether the new covenant supersedes, renews or fulfils the Sinai covenant.

data.statement: Psalm 110 addresses a figure who is declared a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
data.interpretive_divergence: Identification of the addressed figure is contested between traditions.

data.statement: Genesis presents an unconditional promise to Abraham of descendants, land and blessing to the nations.
data.interpretive_divergence: Scope of "blessing to the nations" is interpreted differently across traditions.

data.statement: The Sinai covenant establishes a hereditary Levitical priesthood tied to sacrificial service.
data.interpretive_divergence: Interpretations differ on the continuity of this priesthood after the Second Temple.

data.statement: Hebrews reads the silence of Genesis 14 about Melchizedek's genealogy as significant: "without father or mother… resembling the Son of God."
data.interpretive_divergence: Whether the argument from silence is a rhetorical device, a Second Temple exegetical convention, or a claim about Melchizedek's nature is contested.

data.statement: Hebrews argues that a change of priesthood necessarily entails a change of law.
data.interpretive_divergence: Traditions differ on whether "change of law" means abrogation, fulfilment or transformation of the Mosaic law.

data.statement: The Melchizedekian priesthood of Christ supersedes the Levitical priesthood and its sacrificial order.
data.interpretive_divergence: Accepted in most Christian traditions; framed as fulfilment rather than replacement by some; rejected by Rabbinic Judaism; qualified by dispensational and post-supersessionist readings.
